title: Disruptive Closes $10 Billion Flagship Fund for Ten Late-Stage Bets
excerpt: The Dallas firm founded by Alex Davis is abandoning deal-by-deal vehicles for its first pooled fund, planning checks of up to $1 billion each in AI, defense and software companies.
body:
• Disruptive announced a $10 billion Flagship Fund on October 27, 2026, to back approximately 10 growth and late-stage private technology companies, investing up to $1 billion per company.
  • The vehicle is the firm's first blind-pool fund, replacing the deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles it has used since its founding in 2012.
  • TechCrunch reported the fund is one of the biggest fundraises of the year and, according to the Dallas Business Journal, the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.
  • Disruptive told limited partners it has returned more than $6 billion on roughly $1.9 billion invested, according to Bloomberg reporting cited by TechCrunch.

Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive announced on Tuesday a $10 billion fund to make concentrated bets on late-stage private technology companies, in one of the largest venture fundraises of the year. The firm said the Disruptive Flagship Fund will back approximately 10 companies, with investments of up to $1 billion each, focused on artificial intelligence, defense and software.

TechCrunch reported that the fund aims at capital-intensive fields including AI and defense, and that The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the vehicle, by which point it had already secured at least $7.5 billion in commitments.

A break with the SPV model

The fund is a structural change as much as a fundraising milestone. Until now, Disruptive raised money deal by deal through special purpose vehicles, or SPVs, in which investors back a specific company. The new vehicle is a blind-pool fund: investors commit capital without knowing in advance which companies it will back, and the firm deploys the money at its discretion.

https://x.com/tldrnewsletter/status/2115115528725594332

Founder and chief executive Alex Davis told Bloomberg that top founders have grown frustrated with SPVs that obscure who is investing. "The best companies in the world are basically picking who they want to have invest in them," Davis told Bloomberg, according to Dealroom. In a separate account, he said companies staying private longer require larger checks, adding: "We can't write small checks."

Speaking at Venture Dallas 2026 on October 26, Davis said he concluded about six months ago that the firm could no longer write the size of checks it wanted through SPVs, according to D Magazine. He said the new fund was raised entirely from existing limited partners from the past 15 years. Reporting on the fund's backers has described them as sovereign wealth funds, endowments and universities, backing a firm of roughly 30 people.

"The best private technology companies are growing larger, staying private longer and requiring more capital than ever before."

— Alex Davis, Founder and CEO, Disruptive

The track record behind the raise

Disruptive was founded in 2012 by Davis, the grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis. Its past and present portfolio includes Airbnb, Databricks, ElevenLabs, Helsing, Groq, Palantir, Reflection AI, Spotify and Shield AI, according to the firm's announcement on PR Newswire. TechCrunch also listed Palantir, Airbnb and Spotify among its earlier bets, and chip startup Groq and AI voice startup ElevenLabs among its recent headlines.

Bloomberg reported that the firm told limited partners it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups. D Magazine gave the same figures in its account of Davis's Venture Dallas appearance, where Davis also said he plans to relocate Groq's headquarters to Dallas from Silicon Valley. Davis serves as Groq's executive chairman. Dealroom noted that Groq's chip technology was licensed by Nvidia in a $20 billion deal late last year.

Why the size matters

The firm's own announcement tied the fund's timing to advances in artificial intelligence, the buildout of compute infrastructure and a new era of investment in defense and national security, which it said are creating companies of unprecedented scale and strategic importance while raising the capital required to back them. Disruptive said it invests through primary, secondary and structured transactions. Other reporting on the fund said most capital will go into new funding rounds, with some used to buy shares from existing investors.

The concentration is the strategy and the risk. Putting roughly $1 billion into each of about 10 private companies leaves little room for a weak pick, at a moment when valuations for leading AI and defense companies are climbing and the strongest founders can choose among many large investors.

What comes next

D Magazine reported Davis plans to deploy the $10 billion into about 10 companies over the next 18 months. Which companies take the first checks, and how much goes to existing portfolio names versus new positions, will show whether the pooled structure gives Disruptive the access Davis says SPVs were starting to cost it.
